title: Who built the first knitting machine?
teaches: Hand knitting of stockings in Tudor England; William Lee's stocking frame (1589 by tradition) and the bearded needle; how framework knitting spread to the East Midlands; Strutt's rib attachment; frame rents, cut-ups and the Luddites of 1811 to 1812

blocks.text: In the 1580s, stockings in England were knitted by hand, one loop at a time on a set of needles, often by poor families in their spare hours. A good pair of worsted stockings for a gentleman took days of work. According to a story told in the 17th century, a clergyman named **William Lee** of Calverton, near Nottingham, watched a woman knitting and set out to build a machine that would make a whole row of loops at once.

Lesson 4 showed that knitted cloth is built from rows of loops, each pulled through a loop of the row before. A hand knitter makes these one at a time. Lee's frame, built by tradition in 1589, held a row of fine needles side by side, one for every loop in the row. Each was a **bearded needle**: a hook with a long, springy tip (the beard) that could be pressed into a groove in the straight stem, or shank, to close the hook. With the hook closed, the old loop could slide forward over it and off the needle, onto the new loop caught inside.

blocks.caption: One cycle of the stocking frame on three of its needles. Blue loops belong to the cloth already made; red is the new yarn.

blocks.text: The knitter worked the frame with treadles and hand levers, and each full cycle made a complete row. A frame with hundreds of needles could knit many times faster than a hand knitter, and its loops were more even. The basic movement of the bearded needle was used in knitting machines for more than 250 years, until the latch needle, with a small swinging latch in place of the beard, was patented in England in 1849.

Lee's first frame made coarse woollen stockings. By the traditional account he showed it to Elizabeth I, who refused him a patent, worried that a machine would take work from hand knitters, and perhaps unimpressed that it made wool rather than silk. Lee improved the frame to knit fine silk, but still found no support in England. He took his frames and workers to Rouen in France, with the encouragement of Henri IV, and died in France about 1614. Some of his workers returned to London, and framework knitting grew there. In 1657 the framework knitters received a charter as a London guild that regulated the trade in the City.

Over the 18th century the trade moved to the East Midlands, around Nottingham, Leicester and Derby, where wages and rents were lower and the London company's rules did not reach. Inventors adapted the frame to make other kinds of knitting. In 1759 **Jedediah Strutt** of Derby patented an attachment that made ribbed stockings, which fitted the leg more closely, and the money he made from it later helped finance Richard Arkwright's first cotton mills, as lesson 14 described. By 1800 there were tens of thousands of stocking frames in the East Midlands.

Most framework knitters did not own their frames. They worked at home or in small shops on frames rented from a **hosier**, a merchant who supplied the yarn, paid for finished goods by the piece and charged a weekly **frame rent**, whether there was work or not. In the early 19th century the trade was in trouble. The wars with France cut exports, fashion changed from knee breeches and stockings to trousers, and many hosiers cut piece rates.

Some hosiers also used wide frames to knit large flat pieces of cloth, which were then cut up and sewn into stockings. These **cut-ups** were cheap but fell apart at the seams, and the framework knitters saw them as undercutting both their pay and the good name of the trade. They also complained about masters who took on many apprentices, who could be paid little, instead of trained men.

In March 1811, framework knitters in villages around Nottingham began breaking into workshops at night and smashing frames. They sent letters signed by "General Ned Ludd"[^ned-ludd], an imaginary leader, and they became known as **Luddites**. They did not attack every frame. They chose the frames of hosiers who paid below the agreed rates or made cut-ups, and left others alone. In 1812 the frame breaking spread to the wool districts of Yorkshire and the cotton districts of Lancashire, where croppers, the skilled men who sheared the nap of woollen cloth, attacked shearing frames, and weavers attacked power looms.

The government sent thousands of soldiers into the disturbed counties and, in 1812, made frame breaking a crime punishable by death. In his first speech in the House of Lords, the poet **Lord Byron**, whose family estate was near Nottingham, spoke against the bill, arguing that the frame breakers had been driven to it by hunger. The bill passed, and over the following years dozens of men were hanged or transported to Australia. Today "Luddite" means anyone who opposes new technology, but the original Luddites were protesting about wages, quality and how the machines were used.

blocks.caption: Four questions on the stocking frame.

items.ask: What did Lee's frame do that a hand knitter could not?
choices: Made a whole row of loops in one cycle
Knitted cloth without forming any loops
Wove stockings on a narrow loom
Spun the yarn while it knitted
items.why: One needle per loop, all worked at once, made a complete row each cycle.

items.ask: What is the beard of a bearded needle for?
choices: Closing the hook so the old loop slides over it
Cutting the yarn at the end of each row
Holding the frame's needles evenly apart
Twisting the yarn as it is laid
items.why: Pressed shut, the beard lets the old loop pass over the hook and off, over the new loop.

items.ask: Who paid frame rent, and to whom?
choices: Knitters, to the hosiers who owned the frames
Hosiers, to the Crown for Lee's old patent
Lee's heirs, to the London livery company
Mill owners, to Jedediah Strutt for his rib
items.why: Most knitters rented their frames from hosiers and paid each week, with or without work.

items.ask: What were the first Luddites mainly protesting about?
choices: Low piece rates and cheap cut-up goods
The invention of the stocking frame
The invention of the bearded needle
items.why: They broke the frames of hosiers who cut rates or made cut-ups and spared the others.

summary: **Lee's frame knitted a whole row at once.** Hand knitting made one loop at a time, but the frame, by tradition built in 1589, had one needle per loop.
**The bearded needle closed its own hook.** The old loop slid over the closed hook and off, onto the new loop.
**Framework knitters rented their frames.** Hosiers charged frame rent and paid by the piece, mostly in the East Midlands, where the trade settled in the 18th century.
**Luddites broke chosen frames.** In 1811 they targeted low payers and makers of cut-ups, and in 1812 Parliament made frame breaking a capital crime.

ned-ludd.title: Who was Ned Ludd?
ned-ludd.text: According to a story told in the Midlands, Ned Ludd (or Ludlam) was a young apprentice in Anstey, near Leicester, who in 1779 smashed two stocking frames with a hammer in a fit of anger. Whenever a frame was broken in the years that followed, workers joked that Ned Ludd had done it.
